Part 4 of “How It Actually Works” — a series breaking down the systems every backend engineer depends on but few can explain end to end.

There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. The joke is thirty years old and everyone has heard it. Fewer people can say precisely why invalidation is hard, which is a shame, because the reason is more interesting than the joke.
Caching itself is trivial. Keep a copy of an expensive answer somewhere fast, hand it out instead of recomputing. A junior engineer can add Redis to a service in an afternoon and cut p99 latency by an order of magnitude. It genuinely works, immediately.
The hard part arrives later, and it arrives as an outage.
What a cache actually is
A cache is a deliberate bet that stale data is cheaper than slow data.
That’s the whole idea, and stating it that way makes the trade-off visible in a way that “caching makes things fast” does not. You are choosing to sometimes serve wrong answers in exchange for usually serving fast ones. Every cache decision downstream — TTL, invalidation strategy, eviction policy — is you tuning where on that line you want to sit.
If the data can never be stale, you cannot cache it. Not “you should be careful” — you cannot. Recognizing which data those are is most of the skill.
The two patterns worth knowing
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Cache-aside is what most systems use. Your application checks the cache; on a miss it queries the database, writes the result into the cache, and returns it. The cache is a dumb key-value store that knows nothing about your database.
It’s popular because it’s simple, it degrades gracefully — if the cache dies, everything still works, just slower — and it only caches data someone actually asked for.
Its weakness is a race condition that is easy to miss. Two requests arrive. One reads a value, and before it writes to the cache, another request updates the database and invalidates the cache key. Then the first request finally writes its now-stale value into the empty cache slot. You’ve just cached data that was already wrong, and it will stay wrong until the TTL expires. This is not theoretical — it’s the source of a large share of “why is this user seeing old data” bugs.
Write-through puts the cache in the write path. Writes go to the cache, which writes to the database, and the operation only succeeds when both have landed.
The cache is now never stale, which is a real guarantee. You pay for it with slower writes and a harder failure mode: if the cache is down, writes fail, so the cache became a critical dependency rather than an optimization.
There’s also write-behind, where the cache acknowledges the write immediately and persists to the database asynchronously. Very fast, and it will lose data when the cache node dies mid-flush. Legitimate for metrics and view counters. Not for anything you’d have to explain to a customer.
Why invalidation is genuinely hard
Here’s the part the joke leaves out.
Invalidation is hard because the cache doesn’t know what changed. Your database knows a row was updated. Redis has no idea. Something in your application has to notice the write and translate it into “these specific cache keys are now lies.” That translation is manual, and it’s where the bugs live.
It gets worse with derived data. Say you cache a user’s profile under user:123. Fine — update the user, delete that key. But you also cache their team's member list, a leaderboard they appear on, a search index entry, and a rendered HTML fragment. One database write just invalidated five cache keys, and the coupling between them exists nowhere except in a developer's head. Nothing enforces it. Someone adds a sixth cached view six months later and doesn't know about the other five.
That’s the actual difficulty. Not the mechanics of deleting a key — the fact that the dependency graph between your data and your cached representations of it is implicit, undocumented, and grows every time someone adds a feature.
The other half is that invalidation is distributed. Multiple app servers, multiple cache nodes, sometimes multiple regions. “Delete this key” is a message that can arrive late, arrive out of order, or not arrive at all. There is no transaction spanning your database and your cache, so there is always a window where they disagree. You can shrink it. You cannot close it.
The three failure modes
These have names because they happen often enough to need them.
Stampede (or dogpile). A single very popular key expires. Every request that would have hit the cache now misses simultaneously, and all of them query the database for the same value at the same moment. A cache that was absorbing ten thousand requests per second stops absorbing them instantly, and your database sees the full load without warning.
The fix is to prevent concurrent recomputation. Take a lock so only the first request rebuilds the value while others wait briefly or serve the stale copy. Or refresh proactively — recompute hot keys shortly before they expire, so they’re never actually absent.
Penetration. Requests for a key that exists in neither the cache nor the database. The cache never populates, because there’s nothing to populate it with, so every single request goes straight through to the database. Sometimes it’s a bug; sometimes it’s an attacker deliberately requesting random nonexistent IDs to bypass your cache entirely.
The fix is to cache the absence — store a null marker with a short TTL, so “this doesn’t exist” is itself a cache hit. A Bloom filter in front of the cache does the same job at larger scale.
Avalanche. The nastiest one, and the most preventable. A large population of keys was created at the same moment — after a deploy, a cache flush, or a cold start — so they all carry the same TTL and therefore all expire at the same instant. Your cache hit rate goes from 98% to near zero in one second and the database receives your entire uncached traffic load at once.
The fix costs one line: add random jitter to every TTL. Instead of 3600 seconds, use 3600 plus a random value up to a few hundred. Expiry spreads out and the cliff becomes a slope.
If you take one practical thing from this article, make it the jitter. It is the single highest-value line of caching code most services are missing.
What to actually do
Cache-aside with jittered TTLs handles the overwhelming majority of cases. Start there.
Set TTLs based on how wrong you can afford to be, not on a number that felt reasonable. Ask what happens if a user sees this value sixty seconds after it changed — if the answer is “nothing,” you have your TTL. If the answer involves money or permissions, you probably shouldn’t be caching it at all.
Cache things that are expensive to compute and read far more often than they’re written. A query that runs once per day doesn’t need a cache no matter how slow it is.
And monitor your hit rate. A cache with a 40% hit rate is not an optimization — it’s an extra network hop, an extra failure mode, and an extra source of stale data, paid for with almost no benefit. Plenty of production caches are in exactly that state and nobody has checked.
The one-line summary
Caching is a bet that stale is cheaper than slow. Invalidation is hard not because deleting keys is hard, but because the map from your data to everything you derived from it lives only in your team’s memory.
